newsitem.title: USA: U.S. September payrolls drop, hint slowing economy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. September payrolls drop, hint slowing economy.

text.p: U.S. non-farm payrolls dropped a surprising 40,000 jobs in September, suggesting the economy slowed substantially in the third quarter of the year, Wall Street analysts said.
Weakness in the closely watched economic indicator prompted several experts to predict the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates steady in the near future.
"The number is much weaker than anybody expected," said Jonathan Basile, economist at HSBC Markets Inc. "Obviously the Fed won't do anything on this number," he added.

The Labor Department announced Friday September non-farm payrolls dropped 40,000 against a revised 241,000 jump in August. The unemployment rate rose to 5.2 percent from 5.1 percent in the previous month.
U.S. September factory jobs fell 57,000 while construction and retail rose by 9,000 and 22,000 jobs respectively.
Some analysts said the data could bring U.S. third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to below 2.0 percent after a 4.7-percent advance registered in the second quarter.
"Actually third quarter growth may not even be 2.0 percent, it may not even be 1.5 percent. There is actually a risk of a number closer to zero," Basile said.

Pundits said the drop in U.S. employment gave more credibility to a decision by the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates steady at the last meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in September.
"It's a victory for the Fed in its decision not to raise rates," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
Some analysts expressed concern, however, about a rise to $11.92 in September average hourly earnings from $11.86 in the previous month.
"There is some concern that the average hourly earnings were up more than expected," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc.
"Besides, we're going to have the minimum wage increase added into that next month," Thayer said, referring to a recent approval by Congress of a bill raising the rate.
Some experts said the drop in payrolls hints growth might be slowing, but a rise in wages could still be an inflationary threat. "I think the wage component is still something to watch," Thayer said.
Kevin Flanagan, vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds, agreed, saying that "the wage pressures are something that you have to take note right now."

The U.S. domestic money market cheered up with the data and sent the benchmark 30-year government bond up 1-9/32 minutes after the release. But enthusiasm ebbed a bit later, mostly on rising wage jitters.
About 30 minutes after the release of the numbers, the bellwether bond was up 24/32 at 99-20/32. Its yield was at 6.78 percent, the lowest since August 16.
